analysis.one_liner: Bans former members of Congress from ever lobbying Congress or federal agencies.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in the House Judiciary Committee with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, former senators must wait two years and former House members one year before they can lobby their old colleagues and federal agencies. This bill would make that ban permanent: any sitting member of Congress could never, at any point after leaving office, be paid to lobby Congress or the executive branch. Violating it would be a federal crime.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens, who would no longer see the lawmakers who voted on laws walk across the street to be paid to influence the same laws. Sitting members who don't become lobbyists would also face less competition from ex-colleagues with built-in relationships on Capitol Hill.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters and current members of Congress

how_it_helps.text: Extends the current 'cooling-off' rules — two years for former senators, one year for former House members — into a lifetime prohibition on lobbying Congress or the executive branch.
Makes a violation a criminal offense punishable under the existing federal penalties for post-employment lobbying violations, rather than a mere ethics rule.
Applies to anyone serving in Congress from the 118th Congress onward, so it covers every current and future member rather than being a one-time rule.

analysis.who_pays: Former members of Congress, who would lose a well-trodden and lucrative career path, and the lobbying firms and trade associations that pay premium rates for ex-lawmakers' relationships and institutional knowledge.

drawbacks.text: A lifetime ban is far stricter than the current one-to-two-year rules, and courts have generally been skeptical of broad, permanent restrictions on former officials' employment and political activity, so parts of the bill could face constitutional challenge.

The ban could cut both ways: it also bars former members from representing the government, nonprofits, or ordinary citizens before federal agencies, not just from working for deep-pocketed corporate clients.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — closing the revolving door between writing laws and being paid to influence them — addresses a widely shared public concern, and the cost falls almost entirely on a small group of former officials and the firms that hire them. The main design risk is that a flat lifetime ban is blunt: the existing cooling-off periods exist to balance ethics against the right of former officials to earn a living, and a lifetime bar, with criminal penalties, goes further than any current law. Still, compared with the status quo, the bill's benefits and costs fall on opposite sides of a clean line.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Derrick Van Orden introduced the bill on January 12, 2023.
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary, where no further action was ever taken.
No other member cosponsored the bill during the entire two-year Congress.
Under current law, the post-employment lobbying restrictions are two years for former senators and one year for former House members; the bill would have replaced those with a permanent ban.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Former members of Congress and the lobbying and government-affairs firms that hire them are better off, because the revolving door between Capitol Hill and paid influence work stays open exactly as it was.

for.name: Rep. Derrick Van Orden
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Judiciary Committee.

against.name: House Committee on the Judiciary
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on January 12, 2023 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

against.name: Jim Jordan
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for consideration during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: There was never a vote or a recorded position from either party beyond the lone Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors from either side.

industries.note: The bill would bar their highest-value hires — former members of Congress — from ever lobbying again, cutting off the core product they sell: personal access to the lawmakers who wrote the laws. The status quo keeps that supply of hires available, which is the opposite of what the bill's supporters wanted for the public.

A lifetime lobbying ban would eliminate the best-known post-Congress career path, one that regularly pays several times a congressional salary. Their interest in keeping the door open runs against the public's interest in lawmakers not converting office-holding into paid influence.
